subject: Critical Thinking
title: Logic in AI: How Machines Reason
description: A quick, practical guide to Logic in AI: How Machines Reason.

hook.text: Early AI was pure logic — feed it rules and facts, let it deduce conclusions. It worked brilliantly and terribly.

buildup.text: Expert systems of the 1980s used thousands of if-then rules to diagnose diseases and identify minerals.

discovery.text: The problem: the real world is messy. Pure logic can't handle uncertainty, ambiguity, or common sense.

twist.text: Modern AI (neural networks) abandoned formal logic for pattern recognition — and it works far better.

climax.text: Today's frontier: combining neural networks' pattern skills with logic's reasoning power. The best of both.

punchline.text: AI started with logic, abandoned it, and now needs it back.

quiz.question: Why did early logic-based AI struggle with real-world problems?
options: The real world has too much uncertainty and ambiguity

details.summary: Artificial intelligence uses formal logic as a foundation for automated reasoning, from rule-based expert systems to probabilistic inference in machine learning. The evolution of AI mirrors the evolution of logic itself.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding how AI reasons logically helps evaluate its strengths and limitations, especially as automated systems increasingly make decisions that affect human lives.
takeaways: Early AI was built on symbolic logic and rule-based systems
Modern AI also uses statistical and probabilistic reasoning
Logical transparency remains a challenge for neural network-based AI

faq.question: How do modern AI systems use logic differently from early AI?
faq.answer: Early AI used explicit logical rules programmed by humans. Modern systems learn statistical patterns from data, which is powerful but makes their reasoning opaque and hard to audit.

faq.question: Why is logical explainability important for AI systems?
faq.answer: If an AI cannot explain its reasoning, users cannot verify its conclusions, detect errors, or trust its decisions—especially in high-stakes domains like medicine and law.
